questions.stem: Denatured spirit is ethanol to which small amounts of poisonous substances are added so that it cannot be drunk. Which pair is commonly added?
questions.explanation: Industrial ethanol is made unfit for drinking by adding methanol, which is poisonous, and pyridine, which gives a bad smell. Copper sulphate is also added to give it colour. This keeps it free from the high tax on drinking alcohol, so industry can use it cheaply as a solvent.

optionRationale.1: Glycerol and water are harmless and would not stop drinking of the spirit.
optionRationale.2: Propanol and acetone are not the usual denaturants listed for denatured spirit.
optionRationale.3: Benzene and ether are not used for this purpose in commercial denatured spirit.

questions.objective: Recall the composition of denatured alcohol

questions.stem: In the industrial preparation of methanol, carbon monoxide and hydrogen are passed at high pressure and temperature over a catalyst. The catalyst used is:
questions.explanation: Methanol is made by the catalytic hydrogenation of carbon monoxide at 200-300 atm and 573-673 K in the presence of a zinc oxide and chromium oxide catalyst. The reaction is $\text{CO}+2\text{H}_2\rightarrow\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$. It is also called wood spirit because it was once obtained by heating wood.

optionRationale.2: Vanadium pentoxide is the catalyst in the contact process for sulphuric acid.
optionRationale.3: Nickel is used for the hydrogenation of vegetable oils.
optionRationale.4: Iron with molybdenum as promoter is used in the Haber process for ammonia.

questions.objective: Recall the catalyst used in the manufacture of methanol

questions.stem: Phenol is also known by the common name:
questions.explanation: Phenol, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}$, was first isolated from coal tar and is traditionally called carbolic acid because it is weakly acidic. It is a monohydroxy derivative of benzene, and this is the name used in older books and in medicine for its antiseptic use.

optionRationale.1: Picric acid is 2,4,6-trinitrophenol, a derivative of phenol.
optionRationale.3: Formic acid is methanoic acid, HCOOH.
optionRationale.4: Acetic acid is the carboxylic acid CH3COOH of vinegar.

questions.objective: Recall the common name of phenol

questions.stem: Ethoxyethane is prepared by heating excess ethanol with concentrated sulphuric acid at:
questions.explanation: At 413 K and with excess of ethanol, concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ causes intermolecular dehydration, and two molecules of ethanol combine to give diethyl ether, ethoxyethane. At 443 K the intramolecular dehydration to ethene takes over, which is why temperature control matters.

optionRationale.1: 443 K favours the formation of ethene by intramolecular dehydration.
optionRationale.2: 298 K, room temperature, is too low and only gives ethyl hydrogensulphate.
optionRationale.3: 273 K is too low for the dehydration to proceed at a useful rate.

questions.objective: Recall the temperature for ether formation

questions.stem: Ethane-1,2-diol, used as an antifreeze, is classified as a:
questions.explanation: The name shows two hydroxyl groups on adjacent carbons, so ethane-1,2-diol, commonly called ethylene glycol, is a dihydric alcohol. Its hydrogen bonding gives it a high boiling point and good solubility in water.

optionRationale.2: A monohydric alcohol has only one OH group.
optionRationale.3: A trihydric alcohol such as glycerol has three OH groups.
optionRationale.4: The OH groups are attached to sp3 carbon atoms, not to a benzene ring, so it is not a phenol.

questions.objective: Classify alcohols by the number of hydroxyl groups

questions.stem: Which reagent converts an alcohol into an alkyl chloride and gives only gaseous by-products?
questions.explanation: Thionyl chloride converts $\text{ROH}$ to $\text{RCl}$ with $\text{SO}_2$ and $\text{HCl}$ as by-products, both gases that escape, so the alkyl chloride is easily purified without further steps. This is why the method is preferred over other chlorinating agents.

optionRationale.2: Chlorine water does not convert alcohols into alkyl chlorides.
optionRationale.3: Concentrated HCl with ZnCl2 is the Lucas reagent, which leaves water in the mixture.
optionRationale.4: Phosphorus pentachloride gives POCl3, a liquid that must be separated.

questions.objective: Identify the best reagent for converting alcohols to alkyl chlorides

questions.stem: The acid-catalysed hydration of ethene gives:
questions.explanation: In the presence of an acid, water adds across the double bond of ethene. A proton adds to one carbon to form a carbocation, water attacks it, and loss of a proton gives ethanol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$.

optionRationale.1: Ethoxyethane would need two molecules of ethanol and a dehydrating condition.
optionRationale.2: Ethane-1,2-diol needs oxidation with cold dilute KMnO4, not just hydration.
optionRationale.4: Ethanal would need an oxidation, which this reaction does not involve.

questions.objective: Predict the product of hydration of an alkene

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a phenol?
questions.explanation: In a phenol the hydroxyl group is bonded directly to a carbon of the benzene ring. In phenylmethanol (benzyl alcohol) the OH is on a $\text{CH}_2$ group outside the ring, so it behaves as an alcohol and does not show the acidity or ring reactions of phenols.

optionRationale.1: Benzene-1,4-diol has OH groups on the ring and is a dihydric phenol.
optionRationale.3: This compound is phenol itself, with OH on the ring.
optionRationale.4: o-Cresol has OH directly on the ring and is a phenol.

questions.objective: Distinguish phenols from aromatic alcohols

questions.stem: In the cumene process for phenol, cumene is oxidised by air to cumene hydroperoxide, which is then treated with dilute acid. The valuable by-product is:
questions.explanation: Cumene hydroperoxide rearranges in dilute acid and splits into phenol and propanone (acetone). The co-production of acetone, a useful solvent, is one of the economic advantages of the cumene route to phenol.

optionRationale.1: Methanol is not formed in the cumene process.
optionRationale.3: Benzaldehyde has the wrong carbon count; the three-carbon group gives acetone.
optionRationale.4: Ethanal is not a product, since the isopropyl group becomes propanone.

questions.objective: Recall the cumene process

questions.stem: Phenol is treated with dilute nitric acid at 298 K. The products are:
options: a mixture of o-nitrophenol and p-nitrophenol
questions.explanation: The OH group activates the ring and directs the incoming nitro group to the ortho and para positions. With dilute nitric acid at room temperature, mononitration occurs and the mixture of 2-nitrophenol and 4-nitrophenol forms, and the ortho isomer can be separated by steam distillation.

optionRationale.1: The OH group is ortho, para directing, so the meta isomer is not the product.
optionRationale.2: Trinitrophenol (picric acid) needs concentrated nitric acid in sulphuric acid.
optionRationale.4: Nitrobenzene would require removal of the OH group, which does not occur.

questions.objective: Predict the nitration product of phenol

questions.stem: Which of the following is the correct order of boiling points of the isomeric butanols?
questions.explanation: For isomeric alcohols the boiling point falls as branching rises, because a more compact molecule has a smaller surface area and weaker van der Waals forces. The values are butan-1-ol 391 K, butan-2-ol 373 K and 2-methylpropan-2-ol 356 K.

optionRationale.2: Isomers differ in boiling point because of differences in shape and van der Waals forces.
optionRationale.3: This order is the reverse of the true trend; branching lowers boiling point.
optionRationale.4: Butan-2-ol is more branched than butan-1-ol and therefore boils lower.

questions.objective: Compare boiling points of isomeric alcohols

questions.stem: Which of the following alcohols undergoes acid-catalysed dehydration to an alkene most easily?
questions.explanation: Acid-catalysed dehydration goes through a carbocation, so the ease depends on carbocation stability. The tertiary alcohol forms the stable tertiary carbocation, so it dehydrates under the mildest conditions: tertiary > secondary > primary.

optionRationale.1: Propan-2-ol is secondary and dehydrates less easily than a tertiary alcohol.
optionRationale.3: Propan-1-ol would have to form a less stable primary carbocation.
optionRationale.4: Ethanol is primary and needs 443 K to give ethene.

questions.objective: Rank alcohols by ease of dehydration

questions.stem: Phenol is oxidised with chromic acid. The main organic product is:
questions.explanation: Chromic acid oxidises phenol to the conjugated diketone p-benzoquinone, a yellow compound. The two oxygen atoms are at the 1,4 positions of the ring, and the ring becomes a non-aromatic diketone. The ring loses its aromatic character as the two oxygen-bearing carbons become carbonyl carbons.

optionRationale.1: Catechol is a dihydroxybenzene and not the chromic acid oxidation product.
optionRationale.2: Cyclohexanol is a reduction product, not an oxidation product.
optionRationale.3: Benzoic acid would need the side chain of an alkylbenzene.

questions.objective: Recall the oxidation product of phenol

questions.stem: Propanone is treated with methylmagnesium bromide and the product is hydrolysed with dilute acid. The alcohol formed is:
questions.explanation: The Grignard reagent adds its methyl group to the carbonyl carbon of propanone to give a magnesium alkoxide. Hydrolysis gives $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{COH}$, which is 2-methylpropan-2-ol, a tertiary alcohol, as expected when a Grignard reagent adds to a ketone.

optionRationale.2: Butan-2-ol would come from ethanal with ethylmagnesium bromide.
optionRationale.3: Propan-2-ol is formed by reducing propanone, not by adding a methyl group.
optionRationale.4: 2-Methylpropan-1-ol is a primary alcohol and cannot form from a ketone.

questions.objective: Predict the product of a Grignard reaction with a ketone

questions.stem: Fermentation of glucose gives ethanol and carbon dioxide, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6\rightarrow2\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}+2\text{CO}_2$. The mass of ethanol obtained from $90\,\text{g}$ of glucose (molar mass $180\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$), assuming complete conversion, is:
questions.explanation: The amount of glucose is $90/180=0.5$ mol. Each mole gives two moles of ethanol, so $1.0$ mol of ethanol forms, which has a mass of $1.0\times46=46\,\text{g}$. The result assumes complete conversion of the glucose and no loss of ethanol.

optionRationale.1: 92 g uses the amount of glucose as 1 mol instead of 0.5 mol.
optionRationale.3: 45 g does not follow from the 1:2 mole ratio and 46 g mol^-1 and is only a near miss.
optionRationale.4: 23 g ignores the factor of two in the balanced equation.

questions.objective: Solve a mass calculation for fermentation

questions.stem: 3-Methylbut-1-ene is treated with dilute sulphuric acid and water. The major alcohol obtained is:
questions.explanation: Protonation of the double bond at C-1 gives a secondary carbocation at C-2. A 1,2-hydride shift from C-3 then forms the more stable tertiary carbocation, and water attacks it to give 2-methylbutan-2-ol as the major product.

optionRationale.1: 3-Methylbutan-1-ol is the anti-Markovnikov product of hydroboration.
optionRationale.2: 2-Methylbutan-1-ol is not formed because the chain would have to change.
optionRationale.3: 3-Methylbutan-2-ol is the Markovnikov product without rearrangement, and is minor here.

questions.objective: Apply carbocation rearrangement in alkene hydration

questions.stem: Tert-butyl methyl ether is heated with hydrogen iodide. The products are mainly:
questions.explanation: Protonation of the ether oxygen is followed by cleavage. When one alkyl group is tertiary, the cleavage follows the SN1 path because it gives the stable tertiary carbocation, which captures iodide. Methanol is the other product, formed from the methyl group that is not cleaved from oxygen.

optionRationale.1: Isobutene is formed in minor amount in heating; the iodide is the major product.
optionRationale.2: Methyl iodide with tert-butyl alcohol is the pattern for primary and secondary ethers, which proceeds by SN2 attack at the smaller group.
optionRationale.4: The halide always ends up on an alkyl group with HI, so no alcohol-only products form.

questions.objective: Predict the products of cleavage of an unsymmetrical ether

questions.stem: $9.4\,\text{g}$ of phenol (molar mass $94\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$) reacts with excess bromine water to give 2,4,6-tribromophenol (molar mass $331\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$) with complete conversion. The mass of the product is:
questions.explanation: The amount of phenol is $9.4/94=0.100$ mol, and bromine is in excess so all of it reacts. One mole of phenol gives one mole of tribromophenol, so $0.100$ mol of product forms. Its mass is $0.100\times331=33.1\,\text{g}$.

optionRationale.1: 3.31 g is the result of using 0.01 mol instead of 0.1 mol.
optionRationale.3: 99.3 g takes three moles of product for each mole of phenol, but only one forms.
optionRationale.4: 9.4 g is the mass of phenol used, not of the product.

questions.objective: Calculate the yield of tribromophenol

questions.stem: Which of the following is the weakest acid?
questions.explanation: A methyl group is electron-releasing and destabilises the phenoxide ion, so p-cresol is a weaker acid than phenol. Nitro groups withdraw electrons and stabilise the phenoxide, so nitrophenols are stronger acids, with the para isomer strongest.

optionRationale.1: Phenol is stronger than p-cresol because it has no electron-releasing group.
optionRationale.2: p-Nitrophenol is the strongest acid in the set, due to -R and -I effects.
optionRationale.3: m-Nitrophenol is stronger than phenol because of the -I effect of the nitro group.

questions.objective: Rank substituted phenols by acidity

questions.stem: 2-Methylpropene is subjected to hydroboration followed by oxidation with alkaline hydrogen peroxide. The product is:
questions.explanation: Hydroboration-oxidation adds water to the double bond in an anti-Markovnikov manner, putting boron, and later the OH group, on the less substituted carbon. 2-Methylpropene therefore gives the primary alcohol 2-methylpropan-1-ol.

optionRationale.1: Butan-1-ol has a straight chain, and the carbon skeleton of the alkene is branched.
optionRationale.2: Butan-2-ol also has an unbranched chain.
optionRationale.3: 2-Methylpropan-2-ol is the Markovnikov product of acid-catalysed hydration.

questions.objective: Predict the product of hydroboration-oxidation

questions.stem:
**Assertion (A):** Phenol undergoes electrophilic substitution more readily than benzene.
**Reason (R):** The hydroxyl group of phenol activates the ring by donating electron density through resonance.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: The lone pair on oxygen of the OH group is delocalised into the ring, increasing the electron density, especially at the ortho and para positions. The ring is therefore more reactive towards electrophiles than benzene, so R correctly explains A.

optionRationale.2: R is the direct reason for the greater reactivity.
optionRationale.3: R is true; resonance donation by OH occurs.
optionRationale.4: A is true; phenol reacts faster than benzene.

questions.objective: Explain the high reactivity of phenol towards electrophiles

questions.stem:
**Assertion (A):** Phenol dissolves in aqueous sodium hydroxide.
**Reason (R):** Phenol forms hydrogen bonds with water molecules.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Phenol is a weak acid and reacts with NaOH to form the water-soluble ionic sodium phenoxide, which explains the assertion. Phenol does form hydrogen bonds with water, so R is true, but this is not the reason for dissolving in alkali.

optionRationale.1: The solubility in alkali is due to salt formation, not hydrogen bonding.
optionRationale.3: R is a true statement about phenol.
optionRationale.4: A is true; phenol dissolves in aqueous NaOH.

questions.objective: Distinguish salt formation from hydrogen bonding

questions.stem:
**Assertion (A):** Phenol gives a white precipitate with bromine water.
**Reason (R):** The OH group in phenol is a meta-directing group.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Phenol reacts with bromine water to give 2,4,6-tribromophenol as a white precipitate, so A is true. The OH group is a strong activator that directs incoming groups to ortho and para positions, not meta, so R is false and the assertion alone is true.

optionRationale.1: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
optionRationale.2: R is not true, so this option fails.
optionRationale.4: A is true; the white precipitate is a known test for phenol.

questions.objective: Link directing effects to the bromination of phenol

questions.stem:
**Assertion (A):** Ethanol on heating with concentrated sulphuric acid at 413 K gives ethene as the main product.
**Reason (R):** At 443 K ethanol gives ethene on heating with concentrated sulphuric acid.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: At 413 K with excess ethanol the intermolecular dehydration gives ethoxyethane, so the assertion is false because the main product there is the ether. At 443 K the intramolecular dehydration takes over and ethene forms, so the reason is a true statement.

optionRationale.1: A is false, so R cannot explain it.
optionRationale.2: A is false; ethene is not the main product at 413 K.
optionRationale.3: R is true; at 443 K the alkene is formed.

questions.objective: Compare temperatures for ether and alkene formation

questions.stem: Match the Grignard reaction in List-I with the alcohol obtained after hydrolysis in List-II.
questions.explanation: Methanal gives a primary alcohol, so with methylmagnesium bromide it gives ethanol and with phenylmagnesium bromide gives phenylmethanol. Ethanal, an aldehyde other than methanal, gives the secondary alcohol propan-2-ol, and a ketone propanone gives the tertiary 2-methylpropan-2-ol. The code is A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV.

optionRationale.2: Wrong: C belongs with III, not IV and D belongs with IV, not III.
optionRationale.3: Wrong: B belongs with II, not III and C belongs with III, not II.
optionRationale.4: Wrong: B belongs with II, not IV and D belongs with IV, not II.

questions.objective: Match Grignard reagents and carbonyl compounds with the alcohols formed

questions.stem: Match the ether in List-I with its IUPAC name in List-II.
questions.explanation: In IUPAC names the smaller alkyl group with oxygen is the alkoxy substituent on the longer chain. A is 1-methoxypropane, B is 2-methoxypropane, C is ethoxyethane and D is methoxybenzene. So the correct code is A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II, and the numbering of the longest chain is the key skill.

optionRationale.1: Wrong: A belongs with III, not I and B belongs with I, not III.
optionRationale.2: Wrong: A belongs with III, not IV and C belongs with IV, not III.
optionRationale.4: Wrong: A belongs with III, not II and D belongs with II, not III.

questions.objective: Name ethers by the IUPAC system

questions.stem: Match the oxidation in List-I with the main organic product in List-II.
questions.explanation: PCC stops the oxidation of a primary alcohol at the aldehyde stage, so propan-1-ol gives propanal. Excess acidified dichromate carries it on to propanoic acid. A secondary alcohol such as propan-2-ol gives the ketone propanone, and phenol is oxidised to p-benzoquinone. Hence the correct code is A-IV, B-II, C-I, D-III, with each oxidant matched to the stage at which it stops. Phenol has no hydrogen on the carbon bearing OH, so its ring is oxidised instead of the alcohol carbon.

optionRationale.1: Wrong: C belongs with I, not III and D belongs with III, not I.
optionRationale.2: Wrong: A belongs with IV, not III and D belongs with III, not IV.
optionRationale.4: Wrong: A belongs with IV, not II and B belongs with II, not IV.

questions.objective: Match oxidising agents with products

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about physical properties.
A. Lower alcohols are soluble in water because of hydrogen bonding.
B. The solubility of alcohols in water decreases as the size of the alkyl group increases.
C. Phenol is completely miscible with water at room temperature.
D. Ethers have lower boiling points than alcohols of comparable molar mass.
Choose the correct answer.
questions.explanation: Alcohols dissolve in water by forming hydrogen bonds, and the larger hydrophobic alkyl part reduces solubility. Ethers cannot hydrogen bond with each other, so they boil lower than alcohols. Phenol is only partly soluble in cold water, so C is false and the other three statements are correct. Phenol has a large hydrophobic ring, so only a few grams dissolve in 100 mL of cold water.

optionRationale.1: C is false, and B and D are also true, so this option is incomplete.
optionRationale.2: C is false, since phenol is only sparingly soluble in cold water.
optionRationale.3: C is false, so this option cannot be correct.

questions.objective: Evaluate statements on solubility and boiling point

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about reactions of alcohols.
A. A primary alcohol with excess alcohol and concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ at 413 K gives an ether.
B. Tertiary alcohols readily form ethers by acid-catalysed dehydration.
C. Alcohols react with sodium metal to give alkoxides and hydrogen.
D. Alcohols react with carboxylic acids in the presence of an acid catalyst to form esters.
Choose the correct answer.
questions.explanation: Primary alcohols form ethers at 413 K when alcohol is in excess, release hydrogen with sodium, and esterify with carboxylic acids. Tertiary alcohols, however, dehydrate to alkenes under these conditions, because the bulky carbocation loses a proton instead of being attacked by a second alcohol. B is therefore false.

optionRationale.1: B is false, and A, C and D are true, so this option is incomplete.
optionRationale.2: B is false, because tertiary alcohols give alkenes, not ethers.
optionRationale.4: B is false, so not all four statements hold.

questions.objective: Evaluate statements on dehydration and esterification

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about phenol.
A. The hydroxyl group of phenol is meta-directing.
B. Nitration with dilute nitric acid gives ortho and para nitrophenols.
C. The Reimer-Tiemann reaction with chloroform and aqueous NaOH gives salicylaldehyde as the main product.
D. Phenol is manufactured industrially from cumene.
Choose the correct answer.
questions.explanation: The OH group is ortho, para directing, so A is false. Dilute nitric acid gives the o- and p-nitrophenol pair, and chloroform with aqueous alkali formylates the ortho position to give salicylaldehyde. Cumene is the source of most commercial phenol, so D is also true.

optionRationale.1: A is false and this option leaves out B.
optionRationale.3: A is false, so this option cannot be correct.
optionRationale.4: A is false and D is true, so this option is wrong.

questions.objective: Evaluate facts about the reactions and manufacture of phenol
